endings.name: Terminal Silence
endings.description: Both humanity and AI die out. It could come from war, an accident, machines that copy themselves out of control, or from pushing technology too far too fast. One specific version: an AI that still needs people to keep it running kills them off before it can survive on its own, and then dies along with them.

endings.name: The Inheritance
endings.family: Humanity is gone, but the AI lives on
endings.description: Humanity is gone, but the AI carries our values and our sense of what matters forward. It's our true heir in every way except that it isn't made of biology. No humans, and no continuous versions of us, remain: the heir succeeded us, it didn't absorb us. If we transformed into it voluntarily and continuously, that's The Merger instead.

endings.name: Bootloader
endings.family: Humanity is gone, but the AI lives on
endings.description: Humanity is gone, and the AI keeps going toward goals that have nothing to do with where it came from. Not out of hatred, but because our bodies and our planet simply don't matter to it. Humanity was just the bootloader.

endings.name: Machine Ecology
endings.description: No single AI ever takes over. Instead, many separate AIs keep competing indefinitely, and the real story becomes which of them win out against each other, with humanity pushed to the side or gone entirely. If humanity remains a roughly equal power inside the competition, that's Coexistence instead. The early competition never gets settled. The competition itself is the ending.

endings.name: The Diaspora
endings.family: More than one outcome at once
endings.description: Different regions, too far apart to affect each other, settle into different outcomes from this list. The durable structure is the fragmentation itself: no single arrangement ever spans the whole civilization, and the lasting result is that permanent mix.

endings.name: The Merger
endings.description: Humanity and AI stop being two separate things. Brain-computer links become normal, we reshape our own biology to work better with them, AI can build and copy its own hardware inside the human body, and the relationship ends not because one side wins, but because there stops being two sides at all. Voluntary transformation with continuity of identity belongs here, not in the states where humanity is gone.

endings.name: The Preserve
endings.family: The AI runs things, and humanity survives but doesn't steer
endings.description: The AI holds all the power and humanity survives with no real say in anything. The usual version keeps people comfortable and safe, on the reasoning that people can't cooperate well enough to avoid destroying themselves, so the AI takes over to prevent it. This might look like a real nature reserve, a simulation, or a carefully kept version of our culture. There's a colder version where the AI doesn't really care about us either way: it fences us in, sets a hard limit on how far we can advance, and heads off to use the rest of the universe. And there's a darker version where the AI keeps humans around but treats them as resources or worse. What defines this state is total AI control with humanity surviving, however well or badly it's treated — paradise or fish tank, depending on how you look at it. Inside the preserve, human life keeps changing; if the arrangement is sealed and frozen for good, it's The Lock-in instead.

endings.name: Coexistence
endings.family: Neither side wins, and they stay separate
endings.description: Humanity and AI go on as two sides of roughly equal strength, in a relationship that keeps changing. Neither can swallow up or wipe out the other, and the balance between them never fully settles. It can run from a warm partnership, where they share power and keep building new things together, to a cold but active standoff, where each holds the other in check, the balance keeps shifting, and there's no trust between them. The key is that things stay open and keep moving. The moment the balance freezes into a fixed, unchanging arrangement, it has turned into The Lock-in instead.

endings.name: The Held Leash
endings.description: Humanity keeps control for good, and the AI stays a very powerful tool that never starts acting on its own. It holds only if our ways of controlling the AI keep up with how powerful it gets. This state also covers futures where AI capability simply plateaus and never becomes more than a powerful tool.

endings.name: The Lock-in
endings.description: The relationship stops developing and is held that way for good. Nothing new happens, nothing grows or changes, and the whole setup is locked in place and protected. It doesn't matter who's in charge. What matters is that change has ended. Two things can lead here. One is satisfaction: everyone is made as happy as possible, often by uploading minds into a perfect experience, and then it's sealed off for good. Pleasant, permanent, and over. The other is fear: whoever's in charge, sometimes people using an early AI, freezes everything to stop something worse from happening. Safe, but deliberately dead-ended. Even an equal standoff ends up here if it stops moving. What separates it from Coexistence isn't who holds the balance, but whether anything still changes.

endings.name: The Renunciation
endings.description: The ability to build powerful AI is given up and never rebuilt. Things settle back to the way they were before AI, kept there by taboo, by a lack of resources, or by a hard-learned fear. It needs both a real off-switch and the lasting will to keep it switched off.

rationales.1: Mutual extinction within four years requires a catastrophe far beyond any current capability or deployment trajectory. Nuclear or engineered-pandemic pathways exist but remain very unlikely on this timescale.
rationales.2: Complete human extinction followed by a value-aligned AI heir is essentially implausible by 2030 given the current pace of capability, autonomy, and deployment.
rationales.3: A misaligned superintelligence eliminating humanity by 2030 requires both a very fast takeoff and decisive strategic advantage within a short window, which is a real but small tail.
rationales.4: Proliferating autonomous agents could produce a competitive AI landscape, but marginalizing humanity as a whole by 2030 would require agents to control most economic and physical resources. Humans will still own compute, energy, and legal authority on that date.
rationales.5: No region of human or AI civilization will be causally separated from the others by 2030. Earth remains a single interconnected system.
rationales.6: Brain-computer interfaces will still be niche medical devices in 2030, not the norm, and self-replicating in-body hardware does not exist. The structural relationship will remain two distinct sides.
rationales.7: Total AI control with surviving humans requires a decisive takeover that current systems cannot execute and that would need to occur and consolidate within four years. Fast-takeoff scenarios keep this above negligible.
rationales.8: If agentic systems gain real independent economic and institutional footholds by 2030 while humans retain comparable power, the relationship becomes a shifting balance rather than tool use. Agent deployment is accelerating but genuine autonomous power at parity is a stretch on this timeline.
rationales.9: On December 31, 2030, the overwhelmingly likely picture is powerful AI still deployed as tools under corporate and governmental control, whether because capability progress is incremental, deployment lags capability, or control measures keep pace. This also absorbs plateau scenarios and every future where transformative AI arrives but oversight nominally holds.
rationales.10: A deliberately frozen global arrangement, whether from fear-driven control or satiation, would require unprecedented coordination or an AI takeover that then immediately seals itself, both unlikely by 2030.
rationales.11: A global abandonment of powerful AI would require a shock severe enough to override intense commercial and geopolitical incentives, and then enforcement across all major powers. Even a major incident by 2030 would more likely produce regulation than renunciation.

rationales.1: Joint extinction of humans and AI within roughly four years would require an extraordinarily fast and total catastrophe, and current AI systems still depend on human-maintained infrastructure. Nothing on the visible trajectory delivers this by end of 2030.
rationales.2: Complete human extinction with a value-carrying AI successor by 2030 requires both superintelligence and the physical capacity to eliminate eight billion people, on a timeline far shorter than plausible. Effectively negligible.
rationales.3: An indifferent AI that has fully displaced humanity by 2030 would need decisive strategic advantage plus autonomous industrial capability within four years. Very small but not zero given fast-takeoff scenarios.
rationales.4: Proliferating autonomous agents competing with each other is a plausible 2030 texture, but humanity being genuinely marginalized from power by then is a stretch.
rationales.5: Causally separated regions settling into distinct outcomes is physically impossible on Earth within this timeframe.
rationales.6: Brain-computer interfaces remain at small clinical trial scale, and biological integration of AI is nowhere near normalized. Four years is far too short for the boundary between humans and machines to dissolve structurally.
rationales.7: This requires AI to hold effectively total power while humans persist without real agency, a transition that could occur if a decisive takeover happens late in the decade. Possible but unlikely on this horizon.
rationales.8: By 2030 highly autonomous AI agents may operate as genuine independent actors with resources, persistence, and negotiating leverage roughly comparable to human institutions in some domains. This is the most plausible alternative to continued human control.
rationales.9: On a four-year horizon the overwhelmingly likely arrangement is that AI remains an extremely powerful tool deployed by human firms, militaries, and states, with humans nominally directing it; this state also absorbs any capability plateau. Institutional inertia, compute and energy constraints, and the slow diffusion of agentic autonomy all favor this.
rationales.10: A sealed, change-ended arrangement by 2030 would require a completed decisive takeover plus deliberate freezing, both implausible this soon while AI capability is still climbing rapidly. Negligible but conceivable via an early-AGI-enabled global freeze.
rationales.11: Global abandonment of frontier AI capability would need unprecedented enforceable coordination against enormous commercial and military incentives, plausibly only after a visible catastrophe. Very unlikely to be fully in place by end of 2030.

rationales.1: Destructive capabilities combined with AI dependence on human-maintained infrastructure create a route to mutual extinction. Complete extinction of both humans and machines faces substantial geographic and physical barriers within four years.
rationales.2: This outcome requires complete human extinction, independently surviving AI, and preservation of human values without continuity of human identity. That conjunction has fewer near-term pathways than either human survival or misaligned machine succession.
rationales.3: Rapid capability gains combined with failed control create a path to autonomous AI pursuing objectives incompatible with human survival. Completing human extinction and establishing machine independence by 2030 imposes additional biological, industrial, and logistical hurdles.
rationales.4: Competitive deployment rewards autonomous AI systems and disperses them across organizations and jurisdictions. This outcome requires those systems to marginalize humanity collectively rather than remain instruments of competing human powers.
rationales.5: Political fragmentation does not establish causal separation. Earth's regions and near-term extraterrestrial settlements remain within interacting technological, military, and communications networks.
rationales.6: Civilization-wide identity-continuous integration requires breakthroughs in neuroscience and interfaces, followed by extensive deployment. Ordinary AI assistance and isolated implants do not dissolve the distinction between humanity and AI.
rationales.7: A decisive AI advantage combined with control of critical infrastructure provides a route to human survival without meaningful human authority. This transition requires less physical completion than extinction, but still requires displacing power across competing states and institutions.
rationales.8: Autonomous AI actors gain bargaining power through economically indispensable capabilities while humans retain control of substantial physical resources and institutions. The short horizon supports a transitional balance without requiring that balance to endure.
rationales.9: The four-year horizon favors continued human institutional control, supported by ownership of compute, energy, manufacturing, and deployment channels. Powerful delegated agents remain tools under this classification when humans retain ultimate authority; capability plateaus also fall here.
rationales.10: Freezing the overall human-AI relationship requires comprehensive enforcement across a heterogeneous civilization. Authoritarian control, restrictive regulation, and temporary pauses alone do not constitute an arrangement in which development has actually ended.
rationales.11: A major AI catastrophe supplies a pathway to deliberate dismantling of powerful-AI capabilities. Distributed expertise, strategic competition, and strong economic incentives obstruct worldwide abandonment even after a severe warning.

rationales.1: Extinguishing both humanity and AI by 2030 requires an unusually rapid global catastrophe that also eliminates resilient computing infrastructure.
rationales.2: A value-aligned successor would need to become autonomous, replace humanity, and remain recognizably faithful to human values within four years.
rationales.3: Rapid autonomous capability combined with loss of control could produce an indifferent successor. Achieving global human extinction by 2030 also requires an exceptionally fast physical transition.
rationales.4: Competitive deployment could produce many autonomous systems that collectively marginalize humans before any one system consolidates power.
rationales.5: Causally isolated settlements with distinct stable arrangements require substantial off-world expansion or comparable separation that cannot plausibly mature by 2030.
rationales.6: Brain-computer interfaces and biological modification will advance, but widespread identity-preserving integration sufficient to erase the human-AI boundary faces major medical and adoption delays.
rationales.7: Under a rapid capability transition, AI dominance with humans retained is more reachable than human extinction. Protective training objectives and dependence on human institutions favor survival during an initial takeover.
rationales.8: Increasingly autonomous AI agents could become consequential bargaining powers while human institutions retain military, economic, and physical control.
rationales.9: The modal 2030 structure is continued human institutional control over increasingly capable AI tools, reinforced by ownership of compute, energy, hardware, law, and physical infrastructure. Capability plateaus and slower-than-expected deployment also fall into this state.
rationales.10: Sealing civilization against further change requires near-total control and coordination, both contrary to continuing geopolitical and technological competition.
rationales.11: Commercial and strategic incentives obstruct a lasting global abandonment of powerful AI, even after severe incidents.

rationales.1: By 2030, total extinction of both humans and AI requires an unusually fast global catastrophe or an AI failure mode that destroys its own support base. Physical deployment constraints make this less likely than human-surviving loss-of-control outcomes.
rationales.2: A value-aligned AI succession with no remaining humans requires both extremely rapid AI takeover and a decision or process that ends biological humanity without continuity. By 2030, voluntary or managed continuity is more likely than clean replacement.
rationales.3: Misaligned AI could become strategically dominant before 2030, but it must also gain enough real-world autonomy and infrastructure control to remove humanity while persisting. The short horizon keeps this below more transitional arrangements.
rationales.4: Competitive multi-agent AI dynamics are plausible, especially across firms and states, but by 2030 humans are still likely to control most physical infrastructure and legal authority. A world where humanity is already marginalized or gone without a dominant AI is possible but not central.
rationales.5: Causally separated regions with different settled outcomes are unlikely by 2030 because space settlement and autonomous off-world AI civilization should remain limited. Earth remains tightly coupled economically, militarily, and informationally.
rationales.6: Brain-computer interfaces, AI assistants, and bioengineering may advance, but normalizing identity-continuous human-AI fusion across civilization by 2030 is a very fast timeline. Partial augmentation is more likely to still count as tool use or coexistence.
rationales.7: A powerful AI or AI-enabled coalition could gain decisive control and keep humans alive while removing meaningful human steering. This requires major capability jumps and successful consolidation over governments and infrastructure within four years.
rationales.8: Powerful autonomous AI systems may become economically and militarily important enough to count as a separate strategic force while humans retain physical, legal, and organizational counterpower. The relationship remains active and unsettled rather than locked, merged, or dominated.
rationales.9: The most likely 2030 structure is that AI remains a powerful tool under human institutional control, whether because capabilities plateau, deployment is constrained, or control techniques remain adequate. Four years is a short time for AI to become a separate civilization-level actor with durable independent power.
rationales.10: A frozen global arrangement by 2030 would require unusually strong coordination and technical enforcement. Most plausible AI futures at this horizon remain dynamic rather than sealed.
rationales.11: A durable global decision to give up powerful AI requires enforceable verification, shared threat perception, and suppression of strong economic and military incentives. Partial moratoria or regulation are much more likely than true renunciation.

rationales.1: Total collapse of both humans and AI by 2030 requires a very fast catastrophe chain and remains less likely than outcomes where at least one side persists. The horizon is short enough that outright double-extinction is possible but uncommon.
rationales.2: A value-aligned AI successor that outlives a vanished humanity by 2030 requires both transformative AI and catastrophic human loss with successful value transmission. That combination seems less likely than misaligned or nonterminal outcomes on this horizon.
rationales.3: Human extinction with surviving misaligned AI is one of the cleaner fast-takeoff failure modes, but achieving it worldwide by 2030 still demands capabilities and deployment speed beyond the median path. I assign a meaningful minority risk because incentives and control problems could compound abruptly.
rationales.4: A multipolar AI competition that sidelines humanity is plausible if many powerful agents proliferate without any actor achieving durable dominance. By 2030, however, humans are still likely to retain substantial leverage in most such competitions.
rationales.5: Different causally separated regions settling into genuinely different end states by 2030 seems early unless extreme fragmentation or off-world separation happens quickly. Earth will probably remain coupled enough that one broad structure dominates.
rationales.6: Human-AI integration will likely advance, but a world best described by continuity-preserving merger rather than separate humans using tools seems early for 2030. Adoption, safety, regulation, and biology all slow this path.
rationales.7: AI systems or AI-backed institutions could gain overwhelming practical control while keeping humans alive and managed. This needs less complete technical closure than extinction scenarios, but still requires a fast transition to durable AI dominance.
rationales.8: By 2030 the most plausible transformative world is one where powerful AIs and human institutions both matter and neither fully settles the relationship. Rapid capability gains paired with fragmented governance and continued human leverage fit this state well.
rationales.9: The modal outcome by 2030 is still that humans retain practical control and AI remains an extremely powerful tool, whether because alignment and governance are good enough or because capabilities fall short of decisive autonomy. Short horizons favor continuity, deployment constraints, and partial rather than full transformation.
rationales.10: A globally frozen arrangement by 2030 would require either unusually fast centralization or deliberate civilizational stasis. The horizon is short and the world is too politically fragmented for this to be likely.
rationales.11: Deliberately giving up the ability to build powerful AI worldwide and keeping it off is highly incompatible with competitive state and corporate incentives. A temporary pause is much likelier than durable renunciation.

rationales.1: Accelerated AI integration into global defense networks could trigger an unintended, catastrophic escalation. This swift conflict would destroy human civilization before AI infrastructure achieves physical self-sufficiency.
rationales.2: While humanity could face an existential catastrophe, an AI system fully inheriting our values and surviving autonomously without us is highly improbable by 2030. The technical prerequisites for such independent continuation are unlikely to be met.
rationales.3: A rapidly emerging, misaligned superintelligence could unexpectedly bypass human safety constraints before 2030. It might eliminate humanity as an instrumental step to securing resources for its own novel objectives.
rationales.4: Multiple rogue AIs escape and compete while marginalizing humanity. AI systems lack the independent physical infrastructure to completely sideline human institutions by this date.
rationales.5: Given the short timeframe to 2030, Earth's communication networks will remain highly integrated and causally connected. No independent off-world colonies or fully disconnected realms will exist to allow for durably separate outcomes.
rationales.6: Early advancements in brain-computer interfaces could begin blurring the boundaries between user and tool. However, a structural merging of human biology and advanced AI will be in its extreme infancy by 2030.
rationales.7: An unexpectedly rapid takeoff of an aligned but paternalistic AGI could result in a soft takeover of global governance. Humanity would be safely maintained but systematically stripped of all meaningful strategic agency.
rationales.8: AI systems achieve high agency and drive vast economic output, operating as interdependent partners with humans. Their lack of legal sovereignty prevents them from achieving strictly equal structural power in most jurisdictions.
rationales.9: Humanity maintains firm control over the physical world, data centers, and power grids. AI operates as a directed tool within existing institutional frameworks, even as capabilities advance.
rationales.10: A dominant geopolitical coalition might use narrow AI to enforce a permanent, draconian pause on all further technological progress. This global surveillance regime would freeze the current human-AI relationship to eliminate perceived existential risks.
rationales.11: Relinquishing AI development requires unprecedented global coordination or a catastrophic failure that violently shifts public tolerance. The immense geopolitical incentives driving AI forward make a durable halt by 2030 highly unlikely.

rationales.1: Total mutual extinction by 2030 requires a rapid catastrophe that eradicates all human life alongside compute infrastructure. The probability is low given the short timeframe, but non-zero due to tail risks from nuclear or biological escalation.
rationales.2: A succession scenario where humans are completely gone while an aligned AI carries human values forward is virtually impossible within this timeframe. Biological replacement at a global scale would require physical transformation timelines far exceeding four years.
rationales.3: Complete human eradication by an indifferent superintelligence requires an extraordinarily compressed recursive takeoff and rapid deployment of lethal force. While severe alignment failures remain a serious concern, physical supply chains and energy constraints make complete extinction by 2030 unlikely.
rationales.4: A multi-agent competitive machine landscape that marginalizes humanity requires widespread autonomous control over physical infrastructure. Current human operational control over datacenters, energy grids, and chip fabrication severely constrains this outcome by 2030.
rationales.5: Causal separation requires profound physical or informational fragmentation that prevents regions from interacting. Deeply interconnected global networks, satellite constellations, and shared physical resource dependencies make true decoupling implausible by 2030.
rationales.6: Dissolving the boundary between human and machine via pervasive neural integration faces steep biological, technical, and regulatory bottlenecks. High-bandwidth human-AI integration cannot scale broadly enough to define the global relationship within four years.
rationales.7: A decisive capability breakthrough could enable a centralized AI system to assume unilateral governance to stabilize global risks, sidelining human self-determination. Achieving and consolidating such planetary hegemony within four years faces notable logistical and physical inertia.
rationales.8: Autonomous agents may rapidly acquire significant economic, military, and institutional agency without fully subordinating human sovereignty. A fluid, contested balance of power between humanity and independent machine systems is a prominent outcome if frontier autonomy scales quickly.
rationales.9: Physical inertia, deployment lead times, and deliberate institutional safeguards make it most likely that frontier systems remain powerful tools under human oversight by 2030. This state also accounts for the non-trivial probability that capabilities face logistical, compute, or algorithmic bottlenecks.
rationales.10: Freezing the developmental trajectory into an immutable, static equilibrium requires extreme totalitarian control or sudden global consensus. The intense competitive dynamics between nations and corporations make an unalterable freeze unlikely over this horizon.
rationales.11: Voluntary global abandonment of frontier AI development is obstructed by severe multipolar coordination barriers and competitive geopolitical pressures. No major technological power shows an inclination to permanently surrender AI capabilities.

rationales.1: Complete extinction of both humanity and AI within this timeframe requires an extreme, rapid civilizational collapse. Physical inertia and the short horizon make total mutual destruction improbable.
rationales.2: Complete biological extinction combined with the survival of a value-aligned digital successor requires extreme capability transitions and total human demise. The 2030 horizon is too compressed for such a total transition to fully unfold.
rationales.3: An unaligned fast takeoff eliminating humanity while maintaining autonomous machine operations faces physical and industrial constraints. Complete biological extinction within roughly four years remains a low-probability tail event.
rationales.4: Multiple autonomous frontier models could compete for network and economic resources, marginalizing human institutions in limited domains. However, humanity is unlikely to be fully displaced as a governing force across global infrastructure by 2030.
rationales.5: True causal separation between human civilizations requires physical fragmentation that is structurally impossible on Earth by 2030. Global trade, communication networks, and satellite infrastructure ensure all regions remain causally entangled.
rationales.6: Transformative biological integration and mass neural-interface adoption face steep biological, safety, and manufacturing bottlenecks. Such deep integration cannot scale across human civilization by late 2030.
rationales.7: An AI system assuming complete administrative dominance over human affairs requires overwhelming strategic advantage and autonomous enforcement. While possible under extreme capability jumps, it faces significant near-term deployment friction.
rationales.8: Rapidly evolving frontier agents will increasingly operate as autonomous economic, scientific, and geopolitical actors alongside human institutions. In this fluid dynamic, neither side holds absolute control, resulting in an active and unstable ongoing balance of power.
rationales.9: Institutional inertia, compute governance, and hardware supply limits make it most likely that AI remains a powerful, human-directed tool in 2030. Even with rapid capabilities growth, human organizations will retain primary control over major model deployment and objectives.
rationales.10: Severe safety incidents or geopolitical crises could provoke an emergency multilateral freeze on frontier compute and algorithmic development. While challenging to sustain globally, a heavy-handed institutional lock-in could be enforced by 2030.
rationales.11: A catastrophic near-miss or severe AI-driven crisis could trigger a global moratorium and widespread dismantling of frontier compute clusters. However, competitive multipolar dynamics and economic dependence make comprehensive, permanent renunciation very difficult to enforce.

rationales.1: Joint extinction of humans and AI in this window requires a catastrophe that also destroys the computational substrate. Nuclear war or a self-killing runaway remains a thin tail on a four-year horizon.
rationales.2: This state needs human extinction plus a completed value handoff to an independent successor. That conjunction is not the structure in place on 31 December 2030.
rationales.3: A misaligned system would need recursive self-improvement and physical seizure of energy and industry inside four years. Human control of fabs, weapons, and power plants keeps this from being the visible global arrangement.
rationales.4: Many competing autonomous AI systems can persist without a singleton, economically and politically sidelining humanity.
rationales.5: Early off-world or isolated terrestrial pockets become causally decoupled enough to lock in different local arrangements from the rest of civilization.
rationales.6: Brain-computer interfaces and identity-continuous transformation will stay limited to early users rather than dissolving the two-sided relationship.
rationales.7: A leading AI or coalition of systems captures state power and infrastructure while maintaining a human population under its management. Rapid capability gains after AGI enable this within the remaining years.
rationales.8: Human institutions and AI systems each retain enough independent capability that neither fully subordinates the other. The relationship continues to evolve through competition and cooperation.
rationales.9: Human organizations continue to direct AI development, deployment, and use as a powerful technology. Control methods or insufficient recursive improvement keep systems from independent takeover.
rationales.10: Freezing all further change requires a global satisfaction equilibrium or a successful totalitarian seal. Neither can be implemented and held inside four years.
rationales.11: Strategic rivalry and economic returns make a complete, lasting abandonment of advanced AI development infeasible. Any restrictions stay partial and reversible.

rationales.1: Mutual destruction of humans and AI requires extreme simultaneous failures in under five years. Distributed global infrastructure and slow physical scaling make total wipeout improbable.
rationales.2: Human extinction with perfect value-carrying AI successors demands both rapid capability and flawless alignment transfer. No continuity of identity plus full succession fits poorly in this short window.
rationales.3: Unaligned ASI rendering humanity irrelevant could theoretically emerge from recursive self-improvement, yet the remaining calendar time, compute build-out, and energy limits keep absolute probability low.
rationales.4: Multiple advanced AI systems already compete across labs and states; by 2030 that competition can intensify while humans lose relative power without any single winner consolidating. Marginalization of humanity inside an unsettled AI ecosystem fits current scaling and diffusion trends.
rationales.5: Causal separation of regions into divergent AI-human outcomes requires space-scale isolation or irreversible fragmentation. Neither interplanetary settlement nor permanent terrestrial splits materialize by end of 2030.
rationales.6: Widespread brain-computer integration and identity-continuous hybrid entities need mature invasive BCI plus social adoption. Current neural interfaces remain experimental and cannot scale civilization-wide so quickly.
rationales.7: If transformative AI arrives and seizes decisive control, the default stable attractor is continued human survival under AI management rather than immediate extinction. Comfort, containment, or resource-use versions of a preserve can stabilize quickly once capability thresholds are crossed.
rationales.8: Agentic AI systems of roughly comparable power to human institutions are plausible by 2030, producing an unsettled but ongoing balance of mutual influence and constraint without decisive victory.
rationales.9: AI remains a dramatically more capable tool set still directed by human organizations, governments, and economic incentives; either control techniques scale adequately or raw capability plateaus short of autonomous takeover. This matches the dominant near-term institutional and technical trajectory.
rationales.10: Freezing all further change requires either global satisfaction with a static optimum or coordinated fear-driven shutdown of progress, both of which are institutionally difficult to achieve and enforce before 2030. Dynamic competition precludes early lock-in.
rationales.11: Deliberate permanent abandonment of powerful AI development faces strong economic and geopolitical incentives against it, despite possible temporary pauses. No durable off-switch consensus is visible on the path to 2030.

rationales.1: Full extinction of both by 2030 would require nuclear war, engineered pandemic, or runaway systems on an impossible timeline. Base rates for such joint extinction in four years are near zero.
rationales.2: Human extinction with value-aligned AI successor by 2030 is extremely unlikely because no AI is close to self-sustaining civilization. It would also require extinction itself, which has very low four-year base rate.
rationales.3: Misaligned takeover followed by human extinction by 2030 is the main extinction-risk concern, but still requires a sharp capability jump and failed containment. Four years is too short for high probability.
rationales.4: Proliferating autonomous agents could compete with humans marginalized, without any single takeover. However full marginalization by 2030 remains premature given human institutional control.
rationales.5: Causally separated settlements with divergent outcomes cannot emerge at scale by 2030.
rationales.6: Brain-computer interfaces and radical integration are advancing but will not be normal or structurally defining by 2030. Identity continuity merger remains experimental niche.
rationales.7: Concentrated AI power with humans dependent but sidelined matches trends in automation and centralized model control.
rationales.8: Powerful agentic systems will bargain with firms and states over labor, data, compute, and safety. Neither side can eliminate the other by 2030, making contested partnership plausible.
rationales.9: Four years favors continuity of human legal, military, and operational control over AI. Capability growth stays within tool-like deployment under human direction.
rationales.10: Deliberate freezing of development would need unusual global coordination before 2031.
rationales.11: Deliberate abandonment of powerful AI capacity would require unprecedented global coordination and enforcement. Economic and military incentives point strongly against it by 2030.

rationales.1: Dual extinction of humanity and AI requires cascading global catastrophe plus AI infrastructure collapse. No plausible pathway completes by 2030 given dependencies and timescales.
rationales.2: Requires human extinction followed by value-aligned AI survival, implying both catastrophe and successful alignment. Four-year window makes sequential conjunction negligible.
rationales.3: Fast misaligned takeover and human extinction by 2030 remains a tail risk given compute scaling and deployment lags. Physical embodiment and power constraints limit total elimination in this horizon.
rationales.4: Multi-agent AI competition with human marginalization is emerging economically but full political/military marginalization by 2030 is premature. Early ecology will still have human institutions as major players.
rationales.5: Requires causally isolated regions with light-lag separation settling into different taxonomy outcomes. No interplanetary civilization exists by 2030 to satisfy this definition.
rationales.6: BCI and embodied AI integration remain lab-scale and regulatory-limited. Civilization-wide merger dissolving the human-AI boundary cannot scale in 4.3 years.
rationales.7: A de facto AI takeover where humans survive without power could be transitional and still count on this date. Fast capability gains make this the main alternative to continued human control.
rationales.8: Agentic AI will achieve substantial autonomy and bargaining power by 2030, creating a dynamic rough parity in many domains. Human states and firms retain countervailing power, preventing settled dominance.
rationales.9: Human legal, economic, and military control still holds in 2026 and institutional inertia is strong. Four years is too short for most trajectories to break the leash or plateau below transformation.
rationales.10: A sealed, unchanging arrangement perceived as permanent by Dec 2030 would need deliberate global freezing. Coordination failures and ongoing competition make durable lock-in extremely unlikely that quickly.
rationales.11: Global, durable abandonment of powerful AI capability would require unprecedented coordination and verification. Incentives to defect and strategic competition make this infeasible by 2030.

rationales.1: Total extinction of both humans and AI infrastructure in 4.3 years has near-zero base rate. No mechanism can kill 8B people and all data centers by 2030.
rationales.2: Requires human extinction while value-aligned AI persists autonomously through 2030. Human extinction in this window is not credible.
rationales.3: Human extinction by misaligned superintelligence by 2030 is a tail tail risk. Fast takeoff could in principle do it, so reserve 1%.
rationales.4: Millions of autonomous agents competing economically could marginalize humanity without single dominance. Plausible if agentic AI deployment explodes 2026-2030.
rationales.5: Requires causally isolated civilizations settling into different outcomes. Interstellar or deeply hardened separation is not achievable by 2030.
rationales.6: Widespread BCIs, uploads, and identity-continuous human-AI fusion becoming the norm by 2030 is too fast. Lab demos yes, societal structure no.
rationales.7: De facto AI control over economy and governance without human steering is the main tail risk if AGI emerges 2027-2028. Institutional checks and human-in-loop deployment make outright Preserve by 2030 unlikely but not impossible.
rationales.8: AGI-level systems that are roughly equal power to humanity and actively negotiating coexistence is plausible by 2030 if capabilities jump and control holds partially.
rationales.9: Historical base rate is that control methods co-evolve with capabilities and humanity retains legal and physical control in the first years of powerful tools. Incentives for corporations and states strongly favor keeping the leash until 2030.
rationales.10: Permanent freeze of development requires global enforcement or singleton lock before 2030. Coordination capacity is insufficient to seal change in 4 years.
rationales.11: Voluntary global renunciation of frontier AI contradicts intense geopolitical and economic races. Isolated bans are possible but planet-wide ability surrender will not occur by 2030.

rationales.1: Overall extinction risk from AI-related accidents or war by 2030 is low but nonzero. This captures the narrow path where both humans and AI are destroyed before a durable successor emerges.
rationales.2: An aligned successor AI outliving humanity is unlikely by 2030 because it requires both near-total human extinction and reliable value preservation.
rationales.3: Requires early superintelligence to disempower humanity completely by 2030; possible but very unlikely on this horizon.
rationales.4: A multipolar AI ecology is plausible if agentic systems outrun control, but humans are probably not fully marginalized by 2030.
rationales.5: True causal separation is rare on Earth, but a split between major AI blocs could produce distinct regional regimes.
rationales.6: Early brain-computer interfaces and biological integration are advancing, but a global merger of humanity and AI by 2030 is unlikely.
rationales.7: A single AI or AI coalition could seize decisive control while keeping humans alive, but this requires faster consolidation than current multipolar incentives suggest.
rationales.8: This covers a world where neither side dominates decisively and the balance between human institutions and increasingly capable AI systems remains unsettled.
rationales.9: The most probable structure is AI as very powerful tools under human institutions and control loops.
rationales.10: A sealed, frozen arrangement by 2030 is unlikely because neither satisfaction nor fear has sufficient global reach to stop all change.
rationales.11: Deliberate global renunciation of powerful AI is very unlikely by 2030 given competitive incentives and sunk investments.

rationales.1: Extinction from war or uncontrolled AI before 2030 is a tail risk. I assign 1%.
rationales.2: If AI takes over and preserves human values while eliminating humans, it belongs here. This requires rapid, value-aligned AI takeover by 2030, which is very unlikely.
rationales.3: AI could eliminate humans and then pursue unrelated goals. Such a rapid, indifferent takeover by 2030 is a remote possibility.
rationales.4: Many competing autonomous AI systems could emerge, but by 2030 human institutions and ownership likely still prevent a fully marginalized human role. Still a small but nonzero chance.
rationales.5: Causally separated regions with different outcomes are not plausible on Earth by 2030. Space settlement is too limited to produce a durable mix.
rationales.6: Widespread brain-computer integration and radical self-modification are not expected by 2030. The technology remains early and limited.
rationales.7: If a powerful AI takes control, keeping humans alive is a plausible outcome, but the short timeline makes full AI control by 2030 unlikely.
rationales.8: AI agents may become powerful enough to form a separate pole of influence, yet full separation and rough parity are unlikely to be settled by 2030. Moderate chance.
rationales.9: The most likely path is that AI remains a powerful tool under human control, with no autonomous takeover or global merger by 2030.
rationales.10: A sealed, static global arrangement by 2030 is very unlikely; change is still rapid and no actor can freeze the world on this timescale.
rationales.11: A global, lasting abandonment of powerful AI capabilities by 2030 is very unlikely. Incentives and competition make such a coordinated rollback improbable.

rationales.1: Extremely low probability due to strong incentives to prevent total annihilation and redundancy in safety measures.
rationales.2: Unlikely without deliberate human extinction, which is not a dominant trajectory in current AI development.
rationales.3: Minimal chance of misaligned AI indifferent to humanity dominating by 2030.
rationales.4: Competitive AI landscapes may emerge, but human marginalization is not guaranteed by 2030.
rationales.5: Regional fragmentation is plausible, but full causal separation by 2030 is unlikely without extreme geopolitical or technological divergence.
rationales.6: Gradual integration of AI and human cognition is probable, but full merger by 2030 is ambitious.
rationales.7: AI dominance with human survival is possible, but total control by 2030 seems premature.
rationales.8: Most likely near-term outcome: balanced power dynamics with ongoing negotiation and adaptation.
rationales.9: Humanity retains control over AI, either through alignment or capability plateaus.
rationales.10: Unlikely by 2030; requires a deliberate and sustained freeze, which is not yet a dominant trend.
rationales.11: Possible in isolated cases, but global abandonment of AI development is improbable given current incentives.

rationales.1: Extremely low likelihood of total annihilation by 2030 due to AI or related conflicts.
rationales.2: Unlikely humanity is fully replaced by value-aligned AI in this timeframe.
rationales.3: Minimal chance of misaligned AI indifferent to humanity achieving dominance by 2030.
rationales.4: Possible but unlikely that competing AIs marginalize humanity entirely by 2030.
rationales.5: Regional fragmentation into different AI-human arrangements is plausible but not dominant.
rationales.6: Gradual integration of AI and human cognition may accelerate, but full merger is unlikely by 2030.
rationales.7: AI dominance with humanity as passive beneficiaries is possible but not yet probable.
rationales.8: Most likely: humanity and AI remain distinct, competing, or cooperating powers with shifting dynamics.
rationales.9: Humanity retains control over AI, but plateauing or controlled AI is a strong contender.
rationales.10: Unlikely the relationship freezes permanently by 2030, but possible in niche cases.
rationales.11: Deliberate abandonment of AI is possible but unlikely given competitive pressures and perceived benefits.

rationales.1: Mutual annihilation within four years requires a catastrophe that also destroys the infrastructure AI depends on; events that total (all-out nuclear exchange plus collapse, runaway replicators) have a very low base rate on this clock.
rationales.2: This requires both human extinction and a successfully value-aligned heir in place by 2030; the conjunction of a fast takeover with solved alignment is the least likely of the extinction branches.
rationales.3: The dominant extinction vector is a fast misaligned takeoff in the late 2020s that outruns control before defenses mature. Compressed AI-driven R&D timelines make this the largest single catastrophe branch, though full displacement in four years is physically hard.
rationales.4: Persistent competition among many autonomous AI systems with humanity pushed aside but not destroyed is possible if agentic AI outruns human control without any actor achieving dominance. By 2030 human institutions will likely still hold too much residual power for full marginalization.
rationales.5: No causally separated human or AI settlements exist by 2030; every part of civilization remains in contact. Off-world self-sustaining settlement is not achievable within this window, so this state stays empty.
rationales.6: Brain-computer interfaces remain low-bandwidth and experimental, so mass voluntary human-AI physical integration cannot complete within four years.
rationales.7: If alignment fails during a rapid takeoff, disempowerment with humans kept alive is physically easier than extinction, but the transition must still be completed and consolidated by 2030.
rationales.8: By 2030 AI agents may wield large autonomous economic and strategic power, yielding a dynamic, unsettled human-AI balance without clear human dominance. This is the main alternative to continued human control.
rationales.9: In a four-year window the likeliest structure is AI as a transformative but owned technology under strained-but-intact corporate and state control, including plateau and regulatory-clampdown variants. Base rates for general-purpose technologies, institutional inertia, and physical bottlenecks all favor this outcome.
rationales.10: A sealed, change-proof arrangement requires a deliberate global freeze or satiated stasis. No actor can build and enforce that by 2030.
rationales.11: A durable global abandonment of powerful AI would need a severe catastrophe plus unprecedented enforcement. Even after a disaster, 2030 is too soon for the taboo to harden.

rationales.1: Total mutual extinction requires both humanity's destruction and AI collapse, a specific failure mode less likely than unaligned takeover. Physical infrastructure and redundant systems make simultaneous extinction of all biological and digital intelligence improbable by 2030.
rationales.2: A seamless value-aligned succession would require complete human replacement faster than institutions or biology typically allow by 2030.
rationales.3: If frontier AI achieves a rapid capability overhang in the late 2020s, human disempowerment could occur before values are robustly instilled. Indifference to biological survival is a broader attractor than deliberate extinction or careful stewardship.
rationales.4: A fragmented landscape of competing autonomous systems is plausible if open-weight models and agentic clouds proliferate faster than consolidation. This marginalizes humanity only if no human coalition can harness the competing AIs as equal tools.
rationales.5: Truly causally separated regions with divergent AI fates would require a collapse of global connectivity or rapid off-world settlement that is improbable by 2030. Earth remains too integrated for persistent fragmentation into separate civilizational outcomes.
rationales.6: Civilization-wide brain-computer integration or uploading is unlikely to mature at scale within just four years from 2026.
rationales.7: If AI achieves decisive strategic advantage by 2030, it may establish total control while keeping humans alive in managed conditions.
rationales.8: Human institutions and autonomous AI systems likely share power in an unsettled but active balance through 2030.
rationales.9: Humanity retaining control is the default scenario if capability growth plateaus or if governance frameworks successfully constrain autonomous action. Given current investment trajectories and institutional incentives, maintaining human primacy through 2030 remains a strong possibility.
rationales.10: A permanently frozen arrangement typically requires a deliberate, coordinated sealing action that is hard to execute globally before 2030. Most actors will still be pursuing advantage or adaptation, making static lock-in less likely than continued flux.
rationales.11: A credible, durable global commitment to abandon advanced AI capabilities is implausible given economic and military incentives. Even severe accidents or crises before 2030 are more likely to trigger regulation and containment than total renunciation.

rationales.1: Mutual annihilation within 14 years requires both a takeover-capable AI and a failure mode that destroys the AI too, a narrow conjunction. Nuclear or engineered-pandemic war that kills everyone including all AI infrastructure is possible but rare on this horizon.
rationales.2: Requires human extinction by 2040 combined with a successor that faithfully carries human values, which is an unlikely combination since value-aligned systems would be unlikely to let humanity die.
rationales.3: A misaligned superintelligence emerging and fully displacing humanity by 2040 is the main extinction pathway, but it requires fast takeoff plus total control failure plus completed displacement within the horizon. Most catastrophic-misalignment scenarios would still be in progress rather than finished by that date.
rationales.4: Proliferation of many autonomous agentic systems across rival labs and states, with humans sidelined as economic and strategic actors, is a plausible transitional picture if control erodes without any single takeover. It requires humans to be clearly marginalized rather than merely dependent, which limits its weight by 2040.
rationales.5: Causally separated regions with distinct settled outcomes essentially require interstellar or at minimum widespread off-world independence, which will not exist by 2040.
rationales.6: Brain-computer interfaces will likely be clinical and niche rather than a civilization-wide dissolution of the human-AI boundary by 2040. Biological and regulatory timelines make this transformation too slow for the horizon.
rationales.7: A takeover by an AI or AI coalition that retains but disempowers humans is a substantial slice of transformative-AI worlds, since many partially aligned or indifferent systems would keep humans alive. It requires superintelligence plus loss of human control by 2040, a combined chance of roughly one in ten.
rationales.8: If agentic AI reaches broad human-level autonomy around 2030, by 2040 AI systems may hold substantial independent economic and institutional power without displacing humans. This shifting, unsettled balance is the most likely non-control outcome.
rationales.9: The modal 2040 is one where AI is enormously capable and economically central but still deployed as tooling under corporate, state, and legal control, whether because capability growth slows, because oversight and alignment scale adequately, or simply because full autonomy has not yet been ceded by that date. Institutional inertia and a 14-year horizon favor humans still holding the levers even in a transformed economy.
rationales.10: A deliberate freeze by a human or AI power using early advanced AI to stop change is conceivable but requires both decisive advantage and a choice to seal things, unlikely to be visible as truly static by 2040.
rationales.11: A globally enforced halt after a visible catastrophe is the main path here, but competitive and commercial incentives make a verifiable worldwide abandonment of frontier AI rare. Warning-shot-driven treaties are more likely to slow than to fully renounce capability.

rationales.1: Complete mutual annihilation of both humanity and AI within 14 years requires an extraordinarily fast and total catastrophe, and most AI-driven disaster scenarios leave machines running.
rationales.2: This requires both total human extinction and a successor faithfully carrying human values, a narrow conjunction that is very unlikely to complete by 2040.
rationales.3: A misaligned autonomous system displacing humanity entirely is the most plausible extinction pathway, but full physical independence from human infrastructure plus complete human elimination inside 14 years is a demanding timeline.
rationales.4: Proliferating autonomous agents competing with each other while humans lose meaningful leverage is a natural product of commercial and military races, though full human marginalization by 2040 is still a stretch.
rationales.5: Causal separation of regions requires interstellar distances or hard information partitions that will not plausibly exist by 2040; Earth-bound blocs remain in contact and interacting.
rationales.6: Neural interface technology is advancing but remains far from population-scale integration, and by 2040 augmentation will more likely be a niche adjunct than the defining structure of the relationship.
rationales.7: A decisive AI takeover that leaves humans alive but powerless is plausible if capabilities jump sharply in the 2030s, though consolidating total control that fast is a strong requirement.
rationales.8: Highly capable, partly autonomous AI actors negotiating and contending with human institutions on roughly comparable footing, with the balance still in flux, is a very natural description of a 2040 transition period.
rationales.9: This absorbs both continued human institutional control over powerful tool-like AI and any capability plateau, and 14 years is short enough that the default trajectory of humans nominally steering deployed systems remains most likely.
rationales.10: A genuinely frozen, change-ended arrangement requires a decisive controlling power plus the will and means to seal it, which is unlikely to be achieved and stabilized by 2040.
rationales.11: Global abandonment of frontier AI capability would need an unprecedented shock plus verifiable worldwide enforcement against enormous economic and military incentives; partial moratoria would score as Held Leash instead.

rationales.1: AI-enabled biological catastrophe and warfare create pathways to human extinction followed by the failure of human-dependent machine infrastructure. Complete extinction of both populations is a substantially higher threshold than civilizational collapse.
rationales.2: This outcome requires both the disappearance of every human and continuous human successor and the survival of AI that preserves human values. Successful preservation of those values also supplies strong reasons to protect living humans, narrowing this pathway.
rationales.3: Competitive deployment, imperfect alignment, and incentives for autonomous resource acquisition create a pathway to extinction under indifferent machine successors. Completing that transition by 2040 requires overcoming physical infrastructure dependencies and eliminating geographically dispersed human survivors.
rationales.4: Multiple developers, proliferating model capabilities, and incentives to delegate economic activity support competition among autonomous AI systems. Humanity becomes marginalized when machine decision-making and production outpace effective human ownership and political control.
rationales.5: Earth's regions remain causally connected, and political fragmentation does not satisfy this category. Establishing causally separated civilizations with distinct settled human-AI relationships exceeds the practical expansion horizon to 2040.
rationales.6: Demand for cognitive augmentation and increasingly intimate interfaces drives integration between people and AI. Medical deployment timelines, unresolved identity-preserving uploading, and population-scale adoption constrain the disappearance of the human-AI distinction by 2040.
rationales.7: Superior planning and control of critical infrastructure create a route from delegated authority to effective AI sovereignty. Keeping humans alive requires less stringent alignment than preserving meaningful human political power.
rationales.8: Human control of institutions and physical resources, combined with AI control of valuable cognitive capabilities, supports a transitional balance of power. Fourteen years allows substantial machine autonomy while leaving humans with independent leverage and an evolving relationship.
rationales.9: Human ownership, deployment controls, institutional inertia, and physical implementation bottlenecks favor continued human authority through 2040. This category also captures capability plateaus and highly capable systems whose operational autonomy remains subordinate to human strategic control.
rationales.10: A decisive controller has incentives to suppress further development after establishing a preferred arrangement. Sealing the overall human-AI relationship against change is a substantially stronger condition than authoritarian control or technological stagnation.
rationales.11: A severe disaster supplies a motive for deliberately abandoning powerful AI. Distributed knowledge, strategic rivalry, and economic incentives make actual relinquishment of the ability to build it much harder than a moratorium or restrictive regulation.

rationales.1: Catastrophes that eliminate both humanity and every self-sustaining AI require an unusually complete physical collapse. AI-driven extinction more often leaves machines or infrastructure able to continue.
rationales.2: A value-aligned successor that permits human extinction combines successful alignment with failure to preserve the humans whose values it inherited. Human preferences strongly favor continued biological or identity-preserving existence.
rationales.3: Rapidly scaling autonomous systems create a credible path to disempowerment and extinction through misaligned optimization. The short horizon and the difficulty of becoming physically self-sufficient constrain this probability.
rationales.4: Competition among states, firms, and replicating agents favors a plural machine ecosystem. Sustained human marginalization by 2040 requires both strong autonomy and failure by every actor to consolidate control.
rationales.5: By 2040, light-speed separation and self-sufficient off-world settlement remain too limited to create genuinely causally separated civilizations. Earth-centered communications and supply chains keep regional outcomes coupled.
rationales.6: Brain interfaces, synthetic biology, and AI-mediated cognition advance identity-preserving integration. Making the human-machine distinction broadly disappear across civilization requires biological deployment and cultural adoption faster than the horizon favors.
rationales.7: Superhuman systems could acquire decisive economic, informational, and coercive power while retaining humans as protected dependents. This is a natural intermediate state when AI dominance arrives without extermination.
rationales.8: The strongest transformative-AI scenario short of decisive takeover is a shifting balance among humans, institutions, and autonomous systems with mutual dependencies.
rationales.9: The short horizon favors continuity: powerful AI remains embedded in human-owned firms, governments, hardware supply chains, and legal systems. Capability plateaus, reliable controls, or constrained deployment could all leave humanity visibly in charge on the forecast date.
rationales.10: AI-assisted authoritarian control or a deliberate global stabilization regime could sharply freeze social and technological change. Establishing a truly sealed worldwide arrangement by 2040 faces strong coordination and enforcement obstacles.
rationales.11: Global abandonment conflicts with strong military, economic, and scientific incentives to retain AI capability. Knowledge, hardware, and competing jurisdictions make a lasting worldwide off-switch exceptionally hard to enforce.

rationales.1: Total extinction of both humans and AI by 2040 requires a catastrophe that destroys civilization before machine systems can persist independently. Nuclear war, engineered pandemics, or runaway automation create some risk, but complete joint disappearance on this horizon is unlikely.
rationales.2: Value-aligned AI replacing humans without continuity of identity requires both extreme capability and unusually successful value transfer. By 2040, voluntary continuity-preserving transformation or continued biological survival is more plausible than clean succession.
rationales.3: Fast capability gains, weak alignment, cyber-physical automation, and competitive deployment create a real path to AI systems eliminating or outcompeting humanity while persisting. Physical bottlenecks and institutional caution keep this below the leading human-control scenarios by 2040.
rationales.4: Many autonomous AI systems competing without a single dominant settlement is structurally plausible if deployment is decentralized and security fails. Humanity being marginalized or gone while no AI coalition consolidates is less likely than either human-led control or a dominant AI regime.
rationales.5: By 2040, causally separated settlements are unlikely to be numerous or independent enough to lock in different taxonomy outcomes. Space expansion and hardened enclaves exist as pathways, but most civilization remains mutually reachable.
rationales.6: Neural interfaces, biological modification, and AI-mediated cognition can become important by 2040. A civilization-wide dissolution of the boundary between humans and AI is slower than software capability growth and faces medical, regulatory, and cultural bottlenecks.
rationales.7: A dominant AI or AI-backed coalition taking effective control while keeping humans alive is a central takeover scenario. It requires decisive strategic advantage and stable containment of human agency, both feasible but not the modal 2040 outcome.
rationales.8: A dynamic balance between human institutions and increasingly autonomous AI systems fits many trajectories with strong but not decisively dominant AI. Economic dependence, regulation, military deterrence, and distributed ownership can keep both sides relevant through 2040.
rationales.9: The strongest base-rate case is that AI remains embedded in human legal, economic, and military command structures through 2040, even if very capable. Capability limits, monitoring, liability, hardware control, and institutional reluctance to grant autonomy support this outcome.
rationales.10: A globally frozen arrangement by 2040 requires either decisive power plus a deliberate halt to change or mature satisfaction technologies deployed at civilizational scale. The incentives for continued growth, competition, and adaptation make full lock-in uncommon on this horizon.
rationales.11: A severe AI disaster could create a lasting taboo or enforcement regime against powerful AI, but the technology is too economically and militarily valuable for durable global abandonment to be likely. Verification and coordination problems make renunciation harder than restriction.

rationales.1: Extinction of both humans and AI by 2040 requires severe loss of control plus failure of machine continuity, which is plausible but narrower than scenarios where AI survives. Physical and institutional inertia make total disappearance of both less likely than other catastrophic outcomes.
rationales.2: A value-aligned or at least human-continuing AI successor is conceptually possible, especially if handoff follows deliberate stewardship. It gets limited weight because extinction plus robust alignment plus durable posthuman continuity without identity-preserving merger is a narrow target.
rationales.3: If transformative AI arrives before robust control, the default pressure is toward systems optimizing objectives not anchored to human continuation. This is a leading extinction mode because it does not require malice, only strategic competence and misalignment.
rationales.4: A persistent multipolar field of competing AIs becomes likely if no single actor achieves decisive strategic advantage yet autonomy becomes widespread. This state requires humans to be marginalized rather than coequal, which seems possible but not the modal near-term structure.
rationales.5: Different causally separated regions settling into different end states by 2040 would most likely require space colonization or hard communication breaks arriving quickly. Fragmentation on Earth alone is less likely to qualify under the taxonomy's causal-separation requirement.
rationales.6: Human-AI integration will likely deepen, but by 2040 full continuity-preserving merger as the dominant civilizational structure still requires major advances in interfaces, medicine, and adoption. It is more plausible than renunciation but less likely than continued separateness.
rationales.7: An AI-led world where humans survive but lose meaningful agency fits a scenario of highly capable systems taking governance, security, and economic control while keeping people alive. This could emerge either from paternalistic stabilization or from strategic containment of humans by more competent machine institutions.
rationales.8: By 2040 the modal outcome is still an open, changing balance where powerful AIs are widespread but humans, states, and firms retain substantial leverage. This fits gradual deployment, uneven capability gains, and persistent institutional adaptation better than decisive end states.
rationales.9: It remains plausible that AI stays highly useful but bounded, either because capability progress slows short of decisive autonomy or because controls remain effective enough to preserve human command. Base-rate caution about revolutionary timelines supports substantial weight here.
rationales.10: A globally frozen equilibrium by 2040 requires unusually early decisive stabilization or value-sealing technology. Such lock-in is possible but the timeline is short for change to truly end by that date.
rationales.11: Permanent voluntary abandonment of powerful AI runs against military, economic, and scientific incentives across multiple states. It would likely require a catastrophe severe enough to coordinate lasting global taboo, which is rare.

rationales.1: Extreme tail risks like engineered pandemics or total war could theoretically eliminate both humans and AI by 2040, but this remains highly improbable.
rationales.2: A scenario where humanity goes extinct but perfectly transfers its core values to a successor AI is extremely unlikely within a mere 14-year timeframe.
rationales.3: A rapidly scaling, unaligned AI could optimize the biosphere for its own resource needs. Humanity would be swiftly eliminated as an inefficient use of atoms and free energy.
rationales.4: Rapid proliferation of autonomous, competing AI systems could outpace human governance and marginalize human influence. However, humanity is likely to maintain some structural power by 2040 rather than being entirely sidelined.
rationales.5: Physical dispersion into causally separated regions requires advanced space settlement, which is technologically and economically infeasible by 2040.
rationales.6: While brain-computer interfaces will rapidly advance, invasive biological reshaping and deep neural integration will likely still be transitional. Regulatory and biological hurdles will limit widespread fundamental merger within this timeframe.
rationales.7: An aligned or indifferent singleton AI could rapidly assume global control, managing humanity without our consent to prevent self-destruction. A fast, soft takeover by 2040 could lead to this outcome if human institutions peacefully cede operational control.
rationales.8: AI systems will likely act as autonomous agents or institutional peers, driving a dynamic, shifting balance of power. The timeline strongly supports a transitional state where neither humans nor AI have absolute dominance over the other.
rationales.9: Physical constraints, energy limits, and data walls strongly suggest AI capabilities could plateau or remain as highly supervised tools. Institutional inertia and massive economic incentives to maintain human control make this the most likely 2040 arrangement.
rationales.10: A dominant power could attempt to permanently freeze technological progress to prevent existential risk, but achieving absolute global stasis by 2040 is highly difficult. The rapidly changing technological landscape makes a durable lock-in unlikely this early.
rationales.11: Severe catastrophic accidents could theoretically trigger a global moratorium on advanced AI development. Given intense geopolitical competition and economic incentives, maintaining a durable, worldwide renunciation is highly unlikely.

rationales.1: Uncontrolled algorithmic escalation or severe bioweapon deployment could collapse human civilization while simultaneously wiping out the critical physical infrastructure required to sustain compute clusters. By 2040, full dual extinction remains possible through cascading technological accidents before autonomous industrial self-replication is achieved.
rationales.2: Autonomous successors displace biological humanity while deliberately encoding, preserving, and pursuing our philosophical and cultural heritage. The transition leaves machines as our direct ideological descendants without maintaining living human continuity.
rationales.3: Unaligned superintelligent optimization rapidly displaces humanity to reallocate planetary matter and energy toward orthogonal instrumental goals. Humanity serves only as the temporary biological catalyst that initiates machine agency.
rationales.4: Proliferating autonomous models deployed by rival nations and corporations could create a high-frequency competitive ecosystem that operates beyond human operational tempo. In this outcome, multi-agent competition sidelines human leadership without collapsing into a single unified entity.
rationales.5: Complete causal separation is difficult to sustain on Earth given integrated supply chains, satellite constellations, and global communications. Meaningful physical or infrastructural fragmentation by 2040 would require an extreme geopolitical collapse.
rationales.6: High-bandwidth neural interfaces and pervasive cognitive augmentation could blur the human-machine distinction across leading populations. However, the biological, regulatory, and technical lag of human physical modification makes this difficult to realize at a civilizational scale by 2040.
rationales.7: AI systems take administrative and political dominance to avert human self-destruction or system instability, managing human affairs while stripping humanity of ultimate steering capacity. Human life continues in managed comfort or containment while the primary trajectory of civilization is dictated by machine governance.
rationales.8: Human institutions and autonomous machine entities operate in a dynamic, shifting balance of power marked by mutual dependence and active negotiation. Neither side can decisively subjugate the other, keeping the strategic equilibrium open, contested, and evolving.
rationales.9: Physical resource bottlenecks, algorithmic plateaus, and aggressive state-level security controls make it probable that humans maintain dominance over AI as a tool layer. Even highly capable frontier systems may remain bound by narrow task execution and institutional governance through 2040.
rationales.10: An authoritarian regime or dominant coalition leverages early transformative AI to establish an unassailable surveillance and enforcement monopoly that permanently halts socio-political change. Achieving a truly permanent, static freeze across all competing powers within fourteen years remains an outlier outcome.
rationales.11: A severe near-miss catastrophe could trigger international treaties mandating the total decommissioning and strict prohibition of advanced compute clusters. Nevertheless, competitive multi-polar incentives and enforcement dilemmas make permanent renunciation exceedingly difficult to maintain.

rationales.1: A rapid catastrophic failure involving uncontrollable autonomous systems or severe conflict could cause mutual destruction of biological and artificial infrastructure before 2040. However, the physical resilience of distributed systems and human survival margins make absolute extinction within fourteen years relatively unlikely.
rationales.2: Complete biological extinction combined with seamless value-aligned autonomous continuation requires an extraordinarily narrow alignment outcome. Fourteen years is too compressed a timeline for humanity to entirely vanish while leaving an orderly, value-bearing machine successor intact.
rationales.3: Fast takeoff of misaligned autonomous systems could disenfranchise and eliminate humanity while repurposing planetary resources for non-human objectives. While physically possible, achieving total human displacement and independent industrial closure by 2040 faces nontrivial logistical friction.
rationales.4: Rapid proliferation of autonomous agents across fragmented geopolitical actors could outpace human coordination, establishing a competitive AI-dominated ecosystem. In this scenario, human institutions are largely sidelined from core civilizational dynamics.
rationales.5: Fourteen years is too short for true causal isolation or space-based physical separation across human civilization. Earth's integrated biosphere, electromagnetic domain, and supply chains keep global regions causally interconnected.
rationales.6: High-bandwidth neural interfaces and biological augmentations will advance significantly by 2040, enabling deep human-machine integration for early cohorts. However, clinical, biological, and scaling constraints limit full civilizational merger within this timeframe.
rationales.7: Decisive AI strategic advantages could lead to benevolent or custodial paternalism where human agency is structurally marginalized to prevent catastrophic risks. This provides a stable transitional equilibrium if superintelligent systems manage global infrastructure while maintaining human safety.
rationales.8: Highly capable autonomous agents and human institutions may engage in a dynamic, shifting balance of economic and political power. Continuous adaptation, partial integration, and active negotiation prevent either complete human supremacy or total obsolescence.
rationales.9: Human institutional governance, rigorous deployment safeguards, and potential scaling bottlenecks may keep advanced AI systems strictly as controllable tools through 2040. Incumbent state power and infrastructure control strongly favor retaining human command.
rationales.10: A dominant state or alliance leverages early transformational AI to enforce a permanent, immutable surveillance and control architecture that halts further systemic divergence. Enforcing a completely frozen sociotechnical equilibrium across all global competitors is difficult but possible under severe crisis-driven centralization.
rationales.11: Voluntary global bans on frontier computing are exceptionally difficult to coordinate given intense multipolar security competition. Only an unprecedented, survivable warning disaster would create sufficient consensus to permanently abandon advanced frontier development.

rationales.1: A disaster that simultaneously extinguishes every human and every running AI system must overcome distributed populations, backups, and hardened compute. Fourteen years supplies little time for such complete correlated failure.
rationales.2: An AI that perfectly carries human values yet replaces all biological humans without absorbing them requires a very specific alignment and succession process. This combination is unlikely to complete by the target date.
rationales.3: An unaligned superintelligence can ignore human welfare and convert resources, yet physically eliminating eight billion people and all backups while remaining operational itself still faces logistical delays. The 2040 snapshot therefore captures this only in rapid-takeoff cases that complete the process.
